title: Organisation Learning Plan: Hazira gas terminal release and fire, 2020
audience: Site leadership and the HSE function, planning the learning cascade
status: Learning purposes: not a statutory document. Draft learnings from a ProbeMatrix investigation export; validate them before adoption.

data_quality.text: Draft learnings from an unreviewed analysis: the export's Investigation Status is in_progress and no finding is marked as edited by a person, so this pack stays a draft until the investigation is completed and reviewed.

exclusions.reason: A reviewer voted to downgrade this finding; the Learnings Register leaves it out too.

bottom_line.text: Mechanical Maintenance owns four priority-1 learnings (specification, test, independent check, repeat failures) and is the first function to brief.
Operations & Control Room and Emergency Planning & Command own the isolation learnings: hand-only valves, no isolation criteria and no delegated authority.
Every one of the eleven priority-1 learnings reaches tiers T1 to T4, so frontline, supervisors, managers and site leaders all have something to change.
Deliver site-leadership-coach and supervisor-coach first, then the function and frontline packs, then top management, the board and auditors.

items.text: The findings concentrate in two clusters: Mechanical Maintenance (F02, 194 findings) and Operations & Control Room (F01, 170). Engineering, Design, Documents & MOC (F07, 84), HSE, Process Safety & Audit (F11, 80) and Asset Integrity (F05, 70) follow [FND-91B45FF9; FND-4C645CB5; FND-8083ECAC; FND-303495E9; FND-47B1702F].

items.text: Each tier section below lists up to six of that tier's priority-1 learnings, the ones with the most findings in the tier first; the full set, with every tier's message, is in the Learnings Register and the organisation learning map. Eighty-seven role strings are not yet placed in a tier (T9), so tier counts are a lower bound [FND-B440C1BF].

items.lesson: If you cannot confirm a seal or gasket matches the specification for a pressure part, stop and ask for the spec. Do not fit 'what we normally use'.
items.explanation: If the original specification for a pressure-boundary part is lost and no role owns re-establishing it, maintainers will fit whatever part is to hand, and the substitute becomes normal practice, because the job has to be done and nothing in the system says 'stop'.

items.lesson: After any work that opens a pressure boundary, ask: what test proves this joint, and who witnessed it? Write the answer on the job record.
items.explanation: If no procedure defines how a high-pressure joint is tested before return to service, crews will use the quickest available check (pressurising to operating pressure), and a weak joint will pass, because operating pressure does not prove the joint against the pressures it must withstand.

items.lesson: A flameproof fitting with a missing bolt or open cover is not flameproof. Report it and make it safe the same shift.
items.explanation: If electrical maintenance in hazardous areas responds to breakdowns instead of inspecting explosion-protected equipment, defects that do not stop the equipment working (missing bolts, open enclosures) stay in service until a release finds them.

items.lesson: Ask for practice on the emergencies you are expected to handle. If you have never practised one, tell your supervisor.
items.explanation: If no qualification is defined for control-room operators, people are assigned to emergency duty after general training only, and a rare, time-critical event becomes their first practice, because rostering fills posts with whoever is available.

items.lesson: Treat a gas alarm as late news: the release has already started. Act on it as confirmed until proved otherwise.
items.explanation: If fire and gas detection only lights an annunciator, every protective action depends on people noticing, verifying and deciding, which takes minutes to tens of minutes, because the system was designed to inform rather than act.

items.lesson: If you are fixing the same fault again, say so on the job record. That note is what starts a root-cause review.
items.explanation: If nothing in the maintenance system counts repeat failures on the same item, each failure is fixed as if it were the first, and the same inadequate repair is repeated until it fails in the worst conditions.

items.lesson: Before signing off pressure-boundary work, check the part against a written specification. No spec means no sign-off.
items.explanation: If the original specification for a pressure-boundary part is lost and no role owns re-establishing it, maintainers will fit whatever part is to hand, and the substitute becomes normal practice, because the job has to be done and nothing in the system says 'stop'.

items.lesson: Do not roster anyone alone on emergency duty who has not passed the emergency-response assessment for that unit.
items.explanation: If no qualification is defined for control-room operators, people are assigned to emergency duty after general training only, and a rare, time-critical event becomes their first practice, because rostering fills posts with whoever is available.

items.lesson: Do not accept equipment back from maintenance without a recorded leak/pressure test to the written test pressure.
items.explanation: If no procedure defines how a high-pressure joint is tested before return to service, crews will use the quickest available check (pressurising to operating pressure), and a weak joint will pass, because operating pressure does not prove the joint against the pressures it must withstand.

items.lesson: Know the isolation trigger and the valves for each release scenario on your unit. Do not wait for the call chain to isolate.
items.explanation: If an emergency plan names a release scenario but not who may isolate, and on what criteria, isolation waits for escalation up the chain, because people at the scene reasonably believe they need permission to shut in a major supply.

items.lesson: Include Ex-equipment checks (bolts, covers, glands) in area rounds and record them by item, not as a group.
items.explanation: If electrical maintenance in hazardous areas responds to breakdowns instead of inspecting explosion-protected equipment, defects that do not stop the equipment working (missing bolts, open enclosures) stay in service until a release finds them.

items.lesson: Raise a root-cause request when the same item fails twice in a year.
items.explanation: If nothing in the maintenance system counts repeat failures on the same item, each failure is fixed as if it were the first, and the same inadequate repair is repeated until it fails in the worst conditions.

items.lesson: Write isolation and stoppage criteria, valve lists and delegated authority into the emergency plan for every release scenario.
items.explanation: If an emergency plan names a release scenario but not who may isolate, and on what criteria, isolation waits for escalation up the chain, because people at the scene reasonably believe they need permission to shut in a major supply.

items.lesson: Find every pressure-boundary item with no specification on file and re-establish it (OEM, reverse engineering or an engineered substitute).
items.explanation: If the original specification for a pressure-boundary part is lost and no role owns re-establishing it, maintainers will fit whatever part is to hand, and the substitute becomes normal practice, because the job has to be done and nothing in the system says 'stop'.

items.lesson: List emergency isolation valves that are local-only and assess for each whether a release would deny access.
items.explanation: If the valves that stop a release can only be operated at the valve, they will be unreachable in exactly the event they exist for, because a large release fills the area around them.

items.lesson: Run a monthly repeat-failure report from the CMMS and assign a root-cause analysis to each bad actor.
items.explanation: If nothing in the maintenance system counts repeat failures on the same item, each failure is fixed as if it were the first, and the same inadequate repair is repeated until it fails in the worst conditions.

items.lesson: Define a control-room qualification (knowledge, simulator scenarios, assessment, refresher interval).
items.explanation: If no qualification is defined for control-room operators, people are assigned to emergency duty after general training only, and a rare, time-critical event becomes their first practice, because rostering fills posts with whoever is available.

items.lesson: Define 'replacement not in kind' with examples (seals, gaskets, materials) and make it trigger MOC.
items.explanation: If a management-of-change procedure is published but never triggered, changes in parts, materials and pipework happen without risk review, because people do not recognise a 'like-for-unlike' replacement as a change.

items.lesson: Give shift crews standing written authority to isolate and shut down on defined criteria, and back them when they do.
items.explanation: If an emergency plan names a release scenario but not who may isolate, and on what criteria, isolation waits for escalation up the chain, because people at the scene reasonably believe they need permission to shut in a major supply.

items.lesson: Fund remote-operated (and where justified, automatic) emergency isolation for inventories that can produce a large vapour cloud.
items.explanation: If the valves that stop a release can only be operated at the valve, they will be unreachable in exactly the event they exist for, because a large release fills the area around them.

items.lesson: If responders are not trained to switch from 'locate and fix' to 'isolate from a distance' as soon as a release blocks access, they keep trying to approach and escalate by phone, because that is what normal leak response looks like.
items.explanation: Control-room engineers went out to find the source and were driven back by gas density. Senior shift staff arrived at about 02:35 and could not enter the area; first isolation came at 03:01 and the 36-inch line control valve at 03:04. Responders had no isolation criteria, no remote valves and limited emergency training (see related learnings), so this is a learning about decision support, not individual blame.

items.lesson: Track the number of MOCs raised per month; zero over a long period means the system is not being used.
items.explanation: If a management-of-change procedure is published but never triggered, changes in parts, materials and pipework happen without risk review, because people do not recognise a 'like-for-unlike' replacement as a change.

items.lesson: Require that every shift has at least one qualified emergency-competent person in each control room.
items.explanation: If no qualification is defined for control-room operators, people are assigned to emergency duty after general training only, and a rare, time-critical event becomes their first practice, because rostering fills posts with whoever is available.

items.lesson: Approve and fund F&G voting logic with automatic executive action for major-release areas.
items.explanation: If fire and gas detection only lights an annunciator, every protective action depends on people noticing, verifying and deciding, which takes minutes to tens of minutes, because the system was designed to inform rather than act.

sections.heading: What top management and the board (T5) must learn

items.lesson: Ask for assurance that legacy (pre-2000) pressure equipment has current part specifications and controlled spares.
items.explanation: If the original specification for a pressure-boundary part is lost and no role owns re-establishing it, maintainers will fit whatever part is to hand, and the substitute becomes normal practice, because the job has to be done and nothing in the system says 'stop'.

items.lesson: Ask for evidence that MOC is in active use at each site, not only that a procedure exists.
items.explanation: If a management-of-change procedure is published but never triggered, changes in parts, materials and pipework happen without risk review, because people do not recognise a 'like-for-unlike' replacement as a change.

items.lesson: Ask whether every site's emergency plan says who may isolate, on what criteria, without calling up.
items.explanation: If an emergency plan names a release scenario but not who may isolate, and on what criteria, isolation waits for escalation up the chain, because people at the scene reasonably believe they need permission to shut in a major supply.

items.lesson: Ask for a fleet-wide inventory of local-only emergency isolation valves on major hazard sites.
items.explanation: If the valves that stop a release can only be operated at the valve, they will be unreachable in exactly the event they exist for, because a large release fills the area around them.

items.lesson: If fire and gas detection only lights an annunciator, every protective action depends on people noticing, verifying and deciding, which takes minutes to tens of minutes, because the system was designed to inform rather than act.
items.explanation: Hydrocarbon/H2S detectors were configured annunciator-only, without DCS history and without automatic shutdown or suppression interlocks. The first control-room alarm came at about 02:20, about 7 minutes after CCTV showed the leak and 5 minutes after security staff saw it. The plant relied on a manual chain that took 46 minutes to isolate.

items.lesson: If electrical maintenance in hazardous areas responds to breakdowns instead of inspecting explosion-protected equipment, defects that do not stop the equipment working (missing bolts, open enclosures) stay in service until a release finds them.
items.explanation: The investigating committee identified as the probable ignition source an HPMV flameproof lamp at the skid with three bolts missing and its glass case open about 5-6 cm. Electrical PM was breakdown-skewed, and the post-incident audit grouped all nine lamps into one generic status. Confidence is medium because the ignition source is 'probable', not proven.

items.text: Of the register's 44 recommendations, 24 (55%) sit above the administrative tier: 20 engineering, 2 substitution and 2 elimination. The other 20 are administrative or training. Stronger fixes are missing for two priority-1 learnings: the switch from locating to isolating (LR-08) and control-room competence (LR-12) have administrative and training fixes only, and the register explains why for each [FND-36179046; FND-337CB67F; EVD-6414; EVD-5634].
